title: Buyer Conversation Architectures: Enterprise Personas, Pricing Signals, and Security Objections
author: Eleanor Chen
content:
Overview:
This page defines a collection of conversation architectures (scripted messaging + objection handlers) for common enterprise buyer personas evaluating Redwood Inference. The goal is to give Sales Engineers (SEs) and AEs a reproducible frame for discovery, a compact annotated deck to run a 20–30 minute demo meeting, explicit pricing signals, and a security FAQ tailored for enterprise procurement and infosec reviewers.

Use case: accelerate pilot-to-production conversations where buyers require clarity on latency SLAs, cost economics, and data controls.

Audience: Platform Engineers, ML Engineers, Product Managers, Security/Compliance, Procurement/CFO.

1) Buyer personas and messaging pillars:
- Platform Engineer (primary goal: predictability & ops simplicity)
  - Key message: "Same API, predictable latency, and unified tooling for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
  - Top technical signals: long-tail latency variability, autoscaling complexity, GPU utilization patterns, kernel compatibility requirements.
  - Objections & rebuttals:
    - Objection: "We already run model endpoints on k8s; why a hosted platform?"
    - Rebuttal: "Redwood's runtime reduces 95p tail latency by up to 40% across common LLMs via continuous batching and optimized kernels, cutting orchestration complexity and headcount needed to run at scale."

- ML Engineer (primary goal: output quality and iteration speed)
  - Key message: "Model lifecycle tooling, version pinning, and deterministic rollouts so prompts and evals don't regress in production."
  - Top technical signals: model switches, quantization impacts, KV cache behavior, reproducibility of outputs between variants.
  - Typical objection: "How do I validate quantized variants?"
  - Rebuttal: "We provide per-model quantization profiles plus built-in eval hooks and sampling alignment checks to measure delta against a gold prompt set before rollout."

- Product Manager (primary goal: fastest time-to-value and cost predictability)
  - Key message: "Pilot in days, scale with reserved capacity when needed, and instrument token-level cost to trade quality vs. unit economics."
  - Signals: expected QPS, peak vs median latency requirements, acceptable cost per 1k responses.

- Security/Compliance (primary goal: data residency, auditability)
  - Key message: "Private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs with retention policies compatible with SOC2 requirements."
  - Signals: need for on-prem or VPC, end-to-end encryption, data purge SLA.
  - Objection: "We cannot use any third-party inference"
  - Rebuttal: "Redwood Private runs in-customer VPCs or air-gapped on-prem packages with local key management and audit exports; we can provide an architecture review and template SOC2 evidence."

- Procurement / CFO (primary goal: unit economics and contract flexibility)
  - Key message: "Transition from usage-based pilot to committed Dedicated pools to reduce unit costs with predictable spend and priority capacity."
  - Signals: budget cycle timing, SaaS vs CAPEX preference, contract length.

2) Competitive brief (short form):
- Primary competitors: hyperscale cloud managed endpoints, LLM API providers (general-purpose), and self-hosted inference runtimes.
- Redwood differentiators: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, cost controls (batching, caching, quantization suggestions), integrated rollouts and evals, and opinionated observability (token-level cost and latency).
- Quick counters: 
  - Against cloud managed endpoints: "We provide model-specific kernel selections and KV cache and can yield lower end-to-end token cost for sustained production workloads."
  - Against LLM API providers: "We support private deployments and enterprise-grade auditability which many public APIs cannot offer for regulated workloads."
  - Against self-hosted runtimes: "We remove operational toil (runtime tuning, autoscaling policies, fallback strategies) and provide SLA-backed Dedicated options for critical services."

3) Annotated 10-slide deck (for 20–30 minute meeting):
- Slide 1: Title + customer logo (if allowed) — "Redwood Inference: Predictable Inference for [Customer]"
  - Speaker note: One-line thesis: reduce total cost of serving while preserving quality and compliance.
- Slide 2: Why inference complexity matters — metrics: observed 95p latency, cost per million tokens, ops FTE estimate.
- Slide 3: Buyer-specific impact — pick one persona (platform/ML/product) and map problems -> outcomes (latency down, cost down, time-to-updates).
- Slide 4: Architecture options — Hosted / Dedicated / Private with callouts on control, cost, and deployment speed.
- Slide 5: Runtime features that move the needle — continuous batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization profiles, smart routing.
- Slide 6: Observability and guardrails — token-level cost breakdown, per-model regressions, rollout controls.
- Slide 7: Pricing signals & simple model — pilot pricing, committed capacity tiers, overage mechanics.
- Slide 8: Case study snapshot — 2–3 KPIs from a similar customer (latency, cost, time-to-production).
- Slide 9: Security & compliance summary — VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM, SOC2 / ISO artifacts available.
- Slide 10: Next steps & pilot proposal — timelines, success criteria, contacts.

4) Pricing guidance (SE quick reference) — concise rules of thumb:
- Pilot (0–3 months): Hosted API with consumption pricing and 14-day evaluation credits; typical pilot budget: $2k–$25k depending on QPS and required samples.
- Committed Dedicated (monthly): Discounted unit price for reserved GPU pools; typical commit ranges: $10k/mo (small), $75k–200k/mo (mid/large), multi-year discounts for enterprise.
- Private (one-time + recurring): License + support for on-prem or VPC control plane; usually combined with dedicated committed capacity.

Pricing table (reference):
| Tier | Typical monthly commit | Expected unit price impact | Notes |
| Pilot | $0–$25k | baseline (no commit) | fast start, higher per-token |
| Dedicated-small | $10k | ~20% lower unit cost vs pilot | predictable throughput |
| Dedicated-mid | $75k | ~45% lower unit cost vs pilot | recommended for production ML services |
| Private+Commit | $100k+ | custom | enterprise controls + priority capacity |

Pricing signals to watch during discovery:
- QPS distributions (median vs 95p) — affects batch sizing and pooling economics.
- Average tokens / request — important for per-token math.
- Acceptable tail latency at 95th/99th percentiles.
- Compliance that requires private deployment (moves to a different quote).

5) Pilot activation checklist (SE / Solutions):
1. Discovery: collect QPS, tokens/request, 95p latency target, data residency constraints, and success criteria.
2. Access plan: provide sandbox API key, sample prompts, and a canonical prompt set for evals.
3. Instrumentation: enable token-level cost metrics and latency traces in Redwood Console.
4. Run smoke tests: sample end-to-end flows, verify KV cache warmup behavior.
5. Evaluate: collect prompt-set regression metrics, latency percentiles, and per-token cost over a 7–14 day window.
6. Decision: recommend Dedicated commit thresholds or Private deployment based on observed economics and SLOs.

Success criteria sample (pilot):
- Mean latency <= target (e.g., 150ms for short completions).
- 95p latency improvement >= 20% vs baseline cluster.
- Unit token cost within agreed budget or a clear path to cost parity with commit.

6) Case study (compact):
- Customer: BrightBanc (mid-market fintech) — anonymized composite.
- Problem: High variability in LLM latency causing user-facing timeouts, unpredictable cost on cloud-managed endpoints.
- Solution: Redwood Dedicated with autoscaling policy tuned for peak trading windows, KV caching for common prompts, and a canary rollout for a quantized model variant.
- Outcome (90 day): 95p latency reduced from 1.2s -> 550ms, monthly inference cost reduced 38% after switching to Dedicated commit, time-to-recovery for model regressions reduced from 3 days to <2 hours using integrated evals and rollback.
- Owner: Customer success + SE team; next step: extend to multi-region read replicas for DR.

7) Security FAQ for prospect reviewers (top 10):
- Q1: Where does data persist?
  - A: For Hosted, request payloads are processed in our control plane and logs are retained per contract; for Private, data remains in-customer VPC or on-prem as configured. Retention policies are configurable and we support purge requests with SLA.
- Q2: Can we bring our own keys?
  - A: Yes — Redwood integrates with KMS/HSM providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp HSM). Keys can be customer-managed for encryption at rest.
- Q3: Do you provide audit logs?
  - A: Yes — audit trails include request timestamps, model variant, token counts, user-id (if provided), and rollout events. Logs exportable to SIEM.
- Q4: Is the control plane segregated for customers?
  - A: Private customers get a dedicated control plane. Dedicated customers get tenant isolation plus network controls.
- Q5: What compliance artifacts are available?
  - A: SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 summary, and customer-specific architecture reviews on request.
- Q6: How do you handle data subject requests / deletion?
  - A: We support deletion requests and provide procedures and timelines in the contract. For Private deployments, deletion is customer-controlled.
- Q7: What are your pen test policies?
  - A: Annual third-party pen tests with summaries available under NDA; targeted tests available for enterprise engagements.
- Q8: How do you secure model weights and supply chain?
  - A: We maintain signed model artifacts, verify provenance on onboarding, and provide SBOM-like manifests for runtime dependencies.
- Q9: What networking controls are supported?
  - A: VPC peering, private endpoints, IP allowlists, and egress restrictions for Private deployments.
- Q10: SLA and support response times?
  - A: Hosted: standard support SLA; Dedicated: SLA-backed uptime (typical target 99.9%) and escalation paths; Private: enterprise support with agreed response times in the contract.

9) Appendix: quick links and artifacts to attach in pitch pack:
- Live demo cluster snapshot (with anonymized metrics)
- Sample prompt-set and eval reports (regression delta chart)
- Pricing calculator (spreadsheet)
- Lightweight architecture diagram for each deployment mode (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)

10) Next steps for SEs and AEs:
- Customize the annotated deck to highlight the buyer persona identified in discovery.
- Attach the short case study that most closely matches the industry and scale of the prospect.
- Share pilot plan and success criteria within 48 hours of the meeting; request approval for sandbox credits if needed.
